primaryByRegion.note: Published by WebAIM in prose under 'Primary Desktop/Laptop Screen Reader', not as a table. Percent of respondents in each region whose primary desktop screen reader is JAWS or NVDA. Survey #10 did not report South America.
primaryByRegion.survey11Caveat: This survey had a slightly higher number of respondents from North America where JAWS is more frequently used, but this alone does not account for the notable increase in overall JAWS usage.

publishedProseFigures.text: Beyond JAWS, NVDA and VoiceOver, all other primary screen readers totalled 5.5% (down from 12.2% in 2024).
70.3% use more than one desktop/laptop screen reader; 38.4% use three or more; 15.4% use four or more.
71.6% use more than one desktop/laptop screen reader; 43% use three or more; 17.4% use four or more.
Narrator is the primary screen reader of only 0.4% of respondents but is commonly used by 36.1%.

publishedProseFigures.topic: Reason for use by screen reader
publishedProseFigures.text: 24.3% of NVDA users indicated cost as their primary reason compared to only 1.4% of JAWS users.
Very or somewhat satisfied: NVDA 96.7%, JAWS 95.9%, VoiceOver 90.3%.
Very or somewhat satisfied: NVDA 97.6%, JAWS 95.6%, VoiceOver 92.4%, Narrator 88.9%.
61.9% of JAWS users answered Yes compared with 91.2% of VoiceOver users and 94% of NVDA users.
Frequent use of landmarks/regions (whenever available or often) decreased to 28.3% in 2026 from 31.8% in 2024.
Advanced screen reader users are much more likely to use headings first (72.1%) than beginners (41.4%).
88.3% find heading levels very or somewhat useful (88.8% in Survey #10).
Frequent use of skip links (Always or Often) increased from 31.2% in 2021 to 37.7% in 2026. Survey #10 did not ask this question.
85.6% said PDF documents are very or somewhat likely to pose accessibility issues, up from 75.1% in 2019. Survey #10 did not ask this question.
31.1% said Word documents are very or somewhat likely to pose significant accessibility issues (30.9% in 2019).
Only 8.2% of respondents did not indicate usage of AI in any of the listed ways.
'Better web sites' fell to 83.9% from 85.9% in 2024, the first reversal of a trend running since October 2009 (68.6%).
41% of respondents without disabilities thought the web had become more accessible, against 31.8% of those with disabilities.
Windows usage with primary screen reader increased to 90.7% from 86.1% in 2024.
Preference for mobile apps fell from 58% in 2024 to 54.8% in 2026, reversing an increase over the previous three surveys.

survey10OnlyProblematicItems.note: Survey #10 asked respondents to rank their most problematic items. WebAIM published the order (weighted scores, not percentages). Survey #11 did not ask this question, so there is no 2026 ranking.
rankedItems: CAPTCHA - images presenting text used to verify that you are a human user
Interactive elements like menus, tabs, and dialogs do not behave as expected
Links or buttons that do not make sense
Screens or parts of screens that change unexpectedly
Images with missing or improper descriptions (alt text)
Too many links or navigation items
Lack of "skip to main content" or "skip navigation" links
